data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive inference of future success, but as a methodological rule to maximize the severity of potential falsification; accepting this costs us the assurance that science converges toward truth or that acting on the best-tested theory is 'rational' in the pragmatic sense of maximizing expected utility.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the Tich\u00fd/Miller proof holds, verisimilitude cannot ground the preference, forcing the defense to rely solely on informational content without truth-likeness.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'acting on a theory' (e.g., building a bridge) inherently requires a belief in its reliability/probability, then Popper's distinction collapses into pragmatic induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the cost of being wrong is catastrophic (existential risk), the methodological rule of 'maximizing learning' may be ethically insufficient compared to a precautionary principle based on probable safety.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism reinterprets 'preference' as 'selection for testability.' We choose the better-corroborated theory because it has survived the most severe tests (highest empirical content), making it the most informative target for the next attempt at falsification. This is not a prediction that it will survive the next test (which would be induction), but a strategic choice to learn as much as possible, as fast as possible, regardless of the outcome. The 'action' taken is the commitment to use this theory as the current benchmark for error detection.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
